text: Azure RBAC decides who can do what to which resources, and every permission comes down to one equation. A security principal is the who — a user, a group, a service principal, or a managed identity. A role definition is the what, a collection of permitted actions. Scope is the where, the specific resources it applies to. Change any one piece and you have a different role assignment.

That equation is the single most important mental model for Azure access, and it explains why the same role can mean totally different things depending on where it's assigned — Contributor at a subscription is a much bigger grant than Contributor at one resource group, even though it's the exact same role definition.

Three built-in roles come up constantly. Owner gets full access, including the power to grant access to other people. Contributor also gets full access to manage resources — create, modify, delete — but critically cannot grant access to anyone else. Reader can view everything at the scope but change nothing. That Owner-versus-Contributor distinction is the one people most often get wrong.

Roles can be assigned at four levels, from broadest to narrowest: management group, subscription, resource group, and individual resource. A role assigned at a higher level is inherited by everything underneath it — Contributor at the subscription flows down to every resource group and every resource inside it automatically. Assign it at one resource group instead, and it only applies there.

The principle of least privilege means granting the narrowest role, at the narrowest scope, that still lets someone do their actual job. If Alex only needs to manage VMs in the finance app's resource group, the right call is Contributor scoped to that one resource group — not Owner at the subscription, and not even Contributor at the subscription, which would quietly grant access to every other resource group too.

Put it together: create rg-finance-app, assign the finance security group Contributor at that resource group's scope. They can fully manage everything inside it, they can't touch any other resource group, and they can't grant anyone else access. Exactly the access they need, nothing more.
